claim: Some individuals living with obesity may be relatively metabolically healthy, whilst others suffer from multiple conditions that may be linked to adverse metabolic effects or other factors.
source: Some individuals living with obesity may be relatively metabolically healthy, whilst others suffer from multiple conditions that may be linked to adverse metabolic effects or other factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about obesity heterogeneity that draws from established scientific understanding of metabolic health variability in obesity.

claim: 37 chronic diseases are associated with obesity.
source: We selected 37 chronic diseases associated with obesity and genetic variants associated with different aspects of excess weight.
evidence: The study identified these diseases through literature search of MR studies.

claim: There are 36 FA (favourable adiposity) genetic variants.
source: There are 36 FA variants (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Martin et al., 2021.

claim: FA variants are collectively associated with higher subcutaneous fat but lower ectopic liver fat.
source: We recently identified 36 FA alleles which are collectively associated with a favourable metabolic profile, higher subcutaneous fat but lower ectopic liver fat (Ji et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2021), resembling a polygenic phenotype opposite to lipodystrophy (Semple et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ji et al., 2019, Martin et al., 2021, and Semple et al., 2011.

claim: There are 38 UFA (unfavourable adiposity) genetic variants.
source: There are 38 UFA variants (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by Martin et al., 2021.

claim: UFA variants are associated with higher fat in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, and higher ectopic liver and pancreatic fat.
source: We also identified 38 unfavourable adiposity (UFA) alleles which are associated with higher fat in subcutaneous and visceral adipose tissue, and higher ectopic liver and pancreatic fat (Ji et al., 2019; Martin et al., 2021), resembling monogenic obesity (Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ji et al., 2019 and Martin et al., 2021.

claim: FA and UFA have opposite causal effects on six metabolic conditions.
source: We performed MR studies and showed that FA and UFA have opposite causal effects on six metabolic conditions (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021 and represents findings from previous MR studies.

claim: FA was causally associated with lower risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: While both FA and UFA were associated with higher adiposity, FA was causally associated with lower risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
evidence: This represents findings from previous MR studies by the authors.

claim: UFA was associated with higher risk of type 2 diabetes, heart disease, hypertension, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
source: In contrast, as expected, UFA was associated with higher risk of these conditions.
evidence: This represents findings from previous MR studies by the authors.

claim: 73 genetic variants are independently associated with BMI at genome-wide significance.
source: In the broadest category, we used a set of 73 variants independently associated with BMI at genome-wide significance (p<5 × 10–8). These variants were identified in the GIANT consortium of up to 339,224 individuals of European ancestry (Locke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Locke et al., 2015 and represents data from the GIANT consortium.

claim: 696 variants are associated with body fat percentage in UK Biobank.
source: We used 696 variants from a GWAS in the UK Biobank (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021 and represents GWAS data.

claim: The metabolic effect of higher adiposity is the likely primary cause of coronary artery disease.
source: MR identified two sets of diseases. First, 11 conditions where the metabolic effect of higher adiposity is the likely primary cause of the disease. Here, MR with the FA and UFA genetics showed opposing effects on risk of disease: coronary artery disease, peripheral artery disease, hypertension, stroke, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, chronic kidney disease, renal cancer, and gout.
evidence: This is supported by MR analysis results showing opposing effects of FA and UFA on disease risk, as shown in the figures.

claim: Previous MR studies have provided strong evidence that higher BMI leads to osteoarthritis.

evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous MR studies.

claim: Some MR studies have investigated the effects of fat distribution using genetic variants associated with waist-hip ratio adjusted for BMI.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Emdin et al., 2017, Cornish et al., 2020, and Green et al., 2020.

claim: Adverse fat distribution leads to higher risk of metabolic disease.

evidence: This is a description of the UK Biobank cohort used in the study.

claim: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of urate crystals within the joints.
source: Gout is a form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the deposition of urate crystals within the joints (Dalbeth et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dalbeth et al., 2016 and represents established medical knowledge.

claim: Weight loss from bariatric surgery is associated with lower serum uric acid and lower risk of gout.
source: Weight loss from bariatric surgery is associated with lower serum uric acid and lower risk of gout (Maglio et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maglio et al., 2017.

claim: A previous MR study showed that overall obesity, but not the central location of fat, increased the risk of gout.
source: A previous MR study showed that overall obesity, but not the central location of fat, increased the risk of gout (Larsson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Larsson et al., 2018.

claim: Higher BMI is causally associated with higher risk of osteoarthritis in non-weight-bearing joints including hands.
source: This is consistent with a causal association between higher adiposity and higher risk of osteoarthritis in non-weight-bearing joints including hands (Reyes et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Reyes et al., 2016.

claim: Higher BMI has been shown to be causally associated with higher risk of gallstones.
source: Higher BMI has been shown to be causally associated with higher risk of gallstones (Yuan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yuan et al., 2021.

claim: Higher BMI is a known cause of psoriasis.
source: Higher BMI is a known cause of psoriasis (Budu-Aggrey et al., 2019; Iskandar et al., 2015) and weight loss is a recommended treatment (Iskandar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Budu-Aggrey et al., 2019 and Iskandar et al., 2015.

claim: Weight loss is a recommended treatment for psoriasis.
source: Higher BMI is a known cause of psoriasis (Budu-Aggrey et al., 2019; Iskandar et al., 2015) and weight loss is a recommended treatment (Iskandar et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iskandar et al., 2015.

claim: Higher BMI is listed as a key risk factor for Alzheimer's disease.
source: For example, higher BMI is listed as a key risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (Livingston et al., 2020), although with little evidence of causality, including MR studies that failed to show an effect (Larsson et al., 2017; Nordestgaard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Livingston et al., 2020.

claim: MR studies have failed to show a causal effect of BMI on Alzheimer's disease.
source: For example, higher BMI is listed as a key risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (Livingston et al., 2020), although with little evidence of causality, including MR studies that failed to show an effect (Larsson et al., 2017; Nordestgaard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Larsson et al., 2017 and Nordestgaard et al., 2017.

claim: Recent MR studies have indicated that higher BMI is protective of Parkinson's disease.
source: In contrast to our results, recent MR studies have indicated that higher BMI is protective of Parkinson's disease (Noyce et al., 2017) and causally associated with higher risk of multiple sclerosis (Mokry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noyce et al., 2017.

claim: Recent MR studies have indicated that higher BMI is causally associated with higher risk of multiple sclerosis.
source: In contrast to our results, recent MR studies have indicated that higher BMI is protective of Parkinson's disease (Noyce et al., 2017) and causally associated with higher risk of multiple sclerosis (Mokry et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mokry et al., 2016.

claim: Several MR studies indicate that the association between BMI and many cancers is causal.
source: The reasons why higher BMI is associated with cancers is uncertain, although several MR studies indicate that the association with many is causal (Mariosa et al., 2019; Vincent and Yaghootkar, 2020), and that central adiposity may play a role (Jarvis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mariosa et al., 2019, Vincent and Yaghootkar, 2020, and Jarvis et al., 2016.

claim: Central adiposity may play a role in the association between BMI and cancers.
source: The reasons why higher BMI is associated with cancers is uncertain, although several MR studies indicate that the association with many is causal (Mariosa et al., 2019; Vincent and Yaghootkar, 2020), and that central adiposity may play a role (Jarvis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jarvis et al., 2016.

claim: Some studies have used MR to test insulin directly as a mechanism for cancer risk.
source: Exposure to higher insulin levels is a plausible mechanism, and some studies have used MR to test insulin directly (Nead et al., 2015; Shu et al., 2019; Carreras-Torres et al., 2017b; Carreras-Torres et al., 2017a; Johansson et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Higher adiposity is associated with higher risk of endometrial cancer.
source: Our MR analysis reproduced the previous finding between higher adiposity and higher risk of endometrial cancer (Painter et al., 2016) and renal cell carcinoma (Johansson et al., 2019), and lower risk of breast cancer (Guo et al., 2016; Shu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Painter et al., 2016.

claim: Higher adiposity is associated with higher risk of renal cell carcinoma.
source: Our MR analysis reproduced the previous finding between higher adiposity and higher risk of endometrial cancer (Painter et al., 2016) and renal cell carcinoma (Johansson et al., 2019), and lower risk of breast cancer (Guo et al., 2016; Shu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johansson et al., 2019.

claim: Higher adiposity is associated with lower risk of breast cancer.
source: Our MR analysis reproduced the previous finding between higher adiposity and higher risk of endometrial cancer (Painter et al., 2016) and renal cell carcinoma (Johansson et al., 2019), and lower risk of breast cancer (Guo et al., 2016; Shu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2016 and Shu et al., 2019.

claim: MR studies indicate that higher BMI is protective of postmenopausal breast cancer.
source: The relationship between higher BMI and risk of breast cancer is complicated, with MR studies indicating that higher BMI is protective of postmenopausal breast cancer (Gao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gao et al., 2016.

claim: The protective effect of BMI on breast cancer could be explained by effects of childhood BMI.
source: This contrasts with the epidemiological associations but could be explained by effects of childhood BMI (Richardson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richardson et al., 2020 and represents a speculative explanation.

claim: 21 out of 37 outcome diseases reached an FDR of 0.1 for BMI.
source: We observed 21 out of the 37 outcome diseases reaching an FDR of 0.1 (based on the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure) for BMI, and 19, 11, and 20 out of the 21 diseases causally associated with BMI reaching this FDR for body fat percentage, FA, and UFA, respectively.
evidence: This represents statistical results from the study's MR analyses.

claim: 74 of the 37 × 4 MR tests reached a p-value of <0.05.
source: In addition to correcting for multiple tests, we noted that 74 of the 37 × 4 MR tests reached a p-value of <0.05 when we would only expect 7 by chance, suggesting many of the tests that did not reach a strict Bonferroni p<0.05 were meaningful.
evidence: This represents statistical results from the study's MR analyses.

claim: Many people with higher BMI are at risk of multiple chronic conditions even if their metabolic parameters appear relatively normal.
source: These results emphasize that many people in the community who are of higher BMI are at risk of multiple chronic conditions that can severely impair their quality of life or cause morbidity or mortality, even if their metabolic parameters appear relatively normal.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Higher intra‐abdominal pressure due to excess fat may promote clot initiation and formation in deep vein thrombosis.
source: Possible mechanisms could include higher intra‐abdominal pressure (due to excess fat) and slower blood circulation in the lower limbs (due to a more sedentary lifestyle secondary to obesity, or mechanical occlusion of veins) promoting clot initiation and formation (Lorenzet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to Lorenzet et al., 2012.

claim: Slower blood circulation in the lower limbs may promote clot initiation and formation in deep vein thrombosis.
source: Possible mechanisms could include higher intra‐abdominal pressure (due to excess fat) and slower blood circulation in the lower limbs (due to a more sedentary lifestyle secondary to obesity, or mechanical occlusion of veins) promoting clot initiation and formation (Lorenzet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to Lorenzet et al., 2012.

claim: The protective effect of FA on gout could be due to improved insulin sensitivity leading to less insulin-enhanced reabsorption of organic anions such as urate.
source: The protective effect of FA could be due to improved insulin sensitivity leading to less insulin-enhanced reabsorption of organic anions such as urate (Choi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to Choi et al., 2005.

claim: A sedentary lifestyle and gallbladder hypomotility secondary to increased abdominal fat mass could explain how higher BMI increases the risk of gallstones.
source: These could include a sedentary lifestyle and gallbladder hypomotility secondary to increased abdominal fat mass (Mathus-Vliegen et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to Mathus-Vliegen et al., 2004.

claim: Hepatic de novo cholesterol synthesis could be a metabolic mechanism for gallstones.
source: Metabolic mechanisms could include hepatic de novo cholesterol synthesis (Ståhlberg et al., 1997; Cruz-Monserrate et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to Ståhlberg et al., 1997 and Cruz-Monserrate et al., 2016.

claim: Inflammation is one of the possible causal mechanisms for psoriasis.
source: The non-metabolic pathways could include inflammation which is one of the possible causal mechanisms (Sbidian et al., 2017; Dowlatshahi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citations to Sbidian et al., 2017 and Dowlatshahi et al., 2013.

claim: FA and UFA loci are enriched for genes expressed in adipocytes and adipose tissue.
source: The UFA variants may potentially influence these conditions by load-bearing mechanisms, and tissue enrichment analysis for the FA and UFA variants previously found that FA and UFA loci are enriched for genes expressed in adipocytes and adipose tissue, and mesenchymal stem cells, respectively (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: UFA loci are enriched for genes expressed in mesenchymal stem cells.
source: The UFA variants may potentially influence these conditions by load-bearing mechanisms, and tissue enrichment analysis for the FA and UFA variants previously found that FA and UFA loci are enriched for genes expressed in adipocytes and adipose tissue, and mesenchymal stem cells, respectively (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2021.

claim: Higher BMI at earlier ages may increase bone accrual.
source: This finding adds to the complex relationship between higher BMI and osteoporosis, where higher BMI at earlier ages may increase bone accrual, but in later years results in adverse effects.
